title: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype — working notes / weekly log
linked_artifacts: Slack: incidents thread_1731462200_900114 (queue depth incident / rollback)
content:
Doc purpose
- Working area for the mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short vs long prompts).
- Weekly notes, what we tried, what broke, links to PRs/bench runs, and open questions.
- NOT the final spec (see Confluence design doc + ADR). This is the scratchpad.

Owner / points of contact
- Eng lead: Sofia Ivanova
- Policy design: Lena Fischer
- Implementation: Marcus Reed
- Instrumentation: Julian Moore
- Perf: Omar El-Sayed / Jonas Weber / Rina Kobayashi
- SRE: Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes / Aisha Bello
- Program: Talia Benson

Quick links
- Confluence design: mixed-workload-scheduler-prototype-design
- ADR: adr-0147-short-long-prompt-scheduling-policy
- Benchmark plan: mixed-workload-benchmark-plan
- Perf suite PR: redwood PR #8450, benchmark-lab PR #391
- Canary infra: perf-canary PR #218
- Release note draft: runtime-1-19-mixed-workload-scheduler-flag

High-level goal (restating in one paragraph)
- Reduce p95 tail latency for latency-sensitive / short prompts when co-scheduled with long-context (prefill-heavy) requests.
- Keep throughput regressions bounded and avoid starving long prompts.
- Be stable under bursts; avoid oscillation / priority inversion / pathological batching.

Definitions (the version we’re using in practice, not the academic one)
- “Short” request: interactive-ish; small prefill; can tolerate batching but not sitting behind someone’s 8k+ context.
- “Long” request: prefill dominates; tends to form big contiguous prefill work that inflates tail for everyone.
- “Fairness” in our context: long queue should make progress under sustained mixed traffic; no unbounded wait.

Current prototype shape (as of last edit)
- Two queues: SHORT and LONG.
- Classifier: prompt_tokens threshold + optional predicted prefill cost; later refined with EWMA of observed prefill time.
- Dispatch: short-first BUT with guardrails:
  - periodic long service (fairness window / budget)
  - max-wait bounds / starvation metrics
  - overload admission control by class
- Feature-flagged (default OFF) for runtime-1.19.

Open questions / unresolved (keep this list honest)
1) Classification signal(s)
- Should default split be purely prompt_tokens (cheap + predictable), or do we trust predicted prefill cost enough to use as primary?
- How do we avoid “borderline thrash” when prompt length hovers around threshold? (hysteresis? bucketed thresholds?)
- How do we handle multi-turn chat where prompt_tokens grows during a session? Does the same route see churn?

2) Streaming interactions
- For streaming responses, user-perceived latency is mostly TTFT. Prefill dominates TTFT. We should prioritize TTFT-sensitive work.
- Do we treat streaming as SHORT by default regardless of prompt length? (danger: long streaming summarization jobs…)
- Proposal floating: separate dimension for “interactive vs batch” (hint from route / customer tier), but we said no API changes. Can use internal metadata on some routes.

3) Fairness vs throughput
- What is the acceptable throughput regression at steady state? We’ve been using “<= 3%” as a soft target, but perf standards update may set it explicitly.
- Under 90/10 long/short arrival ratio, do we still prioritize short first? Or do we switch policy when short queue stays empty / low?

4) Pathological batching / kernel confounders
- We saw at least one case where the scheduler change altered batch composition enough to change kernel selection and distort measurements.
- We need to keep kernel choice stable for A/B (or at least capture the reason it changed).

5) Backpressure
- Under overload, is it better to reject/slow LONG earlier to protect SHORT p95?
- What’s the “correct” SRE stance for Dedicated tiers: protect p95 for interactive endpoints at the expense of batch jobs? Probably yes, but needs product alignment.

Experiment log / notes (chronological-ish)

Week of 2024-10-21 (kickoff)
- Goals + scope clarified with perf + SRE.
- Agreed to prototype two-queue policy first (simple, explainable) vs SRPT approximation.
- Action items:
  - Lena: sketch candidate dispatch + fairness windows (ENG-4823).
  - Julian/Omar: define minimal metrics we must have to debug queueing issues (ENG-4824).
  - Rina: update benchmark plan with mixed distributions + trace replay coverage (ENG-4825 / ENG-4830).

Week of 2024-10-28 (classifier v0)
- Marcus started classifier module (redwood PR #8427).
- Default idea: prompt_tokens >= 2048 => LONG, else SHORT.
- Discussion: should output_tokens estimate matter? We decided “not for v0” because decode cost hurts throughput but the tail problem is dominated by prefill blocking.
- Note: we need to store both prompt_tokens and prefill_ms (observed) for later analysis.
- Slack ref: eng-runtime thread_1730482211_104233 (streaming vs non-streaming + threshold bikeshed).

Week of 2024-11-04 (flag plumbing + first dispatch)
- Feature flag plumbing in progress (redwood PR #8421).
- Two-queue dispatch landed behind compile-time guard locally; PR drafted next (became #8433).
- Early microbench: TTFT for short prompts improved in mixed runs, but long prompts got “lumpy” service.
- Worry: if short arrival is constant, long can wait too long. Need explicit starvation mechanism.

Week of 2024-11-11 (two-queue dispatch PR review)
- PR #8433 opened: short-first with fairness window.
- Review notes (from Slack thread_1730759022_883104):
  - Fairness window semantics were ambiguous: “serve 1 long request every N short dequeues” vs “budget of tokens/time”.
  - We should base fairness on time / service cost, not count of requests (long requests are huge).
- Follow-up: adjust to “long service at least once every X ms if long queue non-empty” (more robust under bursty short).

Week of 2024-11-18 (starvation guardrails + instrumentation)
- PR #8439 started: max-wait bound + periodic long service.
- PR #8444 started: tracing spans + metrics.
- Metric naming bikeshed started (thread_1731107744_220901). Current (tentative) names:
  - runtime.scheduler.queue_depth{class=short|long}
  - runtime.scheduler.wait_ms{class=short|long} (hist)
  - runtime.scheduler.service_ms{phase=prefill|decode, class=...} (hist)
  - runtime.scheduler.starvation_events_total{class=long}
  - runtime.scheduler.dispatch_reason{reason=short_first|fairness|max_wait} (sampled logs)
- TODO: confirm label cardinality with telemetry platform (Logan / Caleb). Avoid per-route labels.

Week of 2024-11-25 (first mixed suite run + regression)
- Mixed suite run (local bench harness + early version of benchmark-lab runner):
  - Scenario: 80% short (<=512 prompt), 20% long (>=4096 prompt)
  - Observed: short p95 TTFT improved ~18–25% depending on batch size.
  - Observed: throughput down ~2–4% (varies by model + seq dist)
- Regression case found in one scenario:
  - short p95 got worse when a long prefill formed a batch and short got stuck behind it.
  - Root cause: priority inversion via batching boundary / scheduler lock ordering.
  - Investigation in thread_1730913305_551002.
- Action items:
  - Marcus: repro test + fix (eventually redwood PR #8468).
  - Omar: capture scheduler timeline traces to prove it’s inversion not GPU saturation.

Week of 2024-12-02 (priority inversion fix + backpressure)
- PR #8468: fix priority inversion bug (short requests blocked behind long prefill batch). Added regression test.
- PR #8462: separate admission thresholds by class to prevent long from inflating short queue latency during overload.
- We need to align on “what happens when long is rejected” (429? internal throttle?) — since no API change, this is runtime-level backpressure with existing error surfaces.
- SRE request (thread_1731324499_109883): alerting if long queue starvation is rising OR long queue depth grows steadily during canary (can indicate we over-prioritized short).

Week of 2024-12-09 (benchmark-lab + perf-canary integration)
- benchmark-lab PR #391: standardized runner for mixed workload replay; emits tables + plots (p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util).
- perf-canary PR #218: canary job does baseline vs flag-on A/B and publishes summary.
- We now have enough to do a guarded canary in perf-canary env.
- Notes from Jonas: don’t trust single-run p95 deltas; require N>=5 runs + CI for noise.

Week of 2024-12-16 (EWMA classifier refinement + lock contention)
- PR #8480: use EWMA of observed prefill time to refine split.
  - Safeguards: cap EWMA influence; fallback to prompt_tokens threshold if sparse data.
  - Concern: can learn “wrong” during transient GPU contention; make sure we only update EWMA from low-contention samples? (open)
- PR #8495: lock contention improvements after per-class queues.
  - Before/after: reduced scheduler mutex hold time (measured in profiling) and decreased tail spikes under high QPS.
- Structured logging (PR #8502) added sampled “dispatch decision” events for on-call debugging.

Canary notes (prep + early signals)
- Canary readiness checklist discussion: thread_1731288801_332119.
- Tentative canary success criteria (needs final sign-off w/ SRE + product):
  - Short p95 TTFT improvement >= 10% in at least 2/3 mixed scenarios (or clear improvement in trace replay for representative customers)
  - No new error modes (timeouts, OOM, runaway queue growth)
  - Throughput regression <= 3% (steady-state) OR explained/mitigated
  - Long starvation: runtime.scheduler.starvation_events_total stays ~0; long max wait bounded (define bound per model)
- Rollback triggers (draft):
  - short p95 regression > 5% sustained for > 15 min (relative to baseline slice)
  - queue depth growth without stabilization (either class)
  - elevated timeouts / request cancellations correlated with scheduler flag
  - long wait p99 exceeds bound + rising starvation events

Bench run scratchpad (paste links / IDs here)
- 2024-11-25: local run “mix_80_20_v0” (needs upload)
- 2024-12-03: bench harness “mix_prefill_block_repro” (used for PR #8468 regression test)
- 2024-12-10: benchmark-lab output “mw_trace_replay_setA_r1” (Rina has tables; attach in results sheet)
- TODO: keep this section updated with actual artifact URLs once the runner publishes stable links.

Decisions made (small ones)
- We will NOT introduce new customer-facing hints/params in the prototype.
- Classifier v0 is prompt_tokens threshold; any “smarter” signal must be safe-default and reversible.
- We prioritize TTFT improvements for interactive work, bounded by fairness + throughput constraints.

TODO / next actions (as of 2024-12-19)
- Sofia + Sean: finalize rollback triggers + on-call coverage for canary window (ENG-4829).
- Lena: pick initial fairness parameters (time-based) and document recommended defaults in the heuristics doc.
- Rina: run trace-based replay benchmarks (ENG-4830) with at least 2 customer-like mixes + 2 hardware SKUs.
- Julian: verify metric names and dashboard panels match (ENG-4828); confirm no high-cardinality labels.
- Marcus: land fairness simulation harness gates (PR #8488) and add one burst-oscillation scenario.
- Omar: validate kernel selection stability in A/B; annotate cases where scheduler changes batch shapes materially.
- Talia: start drafting the canary readout template + required evidence list.

Random notes / parking lot
- Fairness parameterization we keep returning to:
  - Option A: “Serve LONG at least once every X ms if long queue non-empty.”
  - Option B: “Allocate Y% of dispatch budget to LONG over sliding window.”
  - Option C: token-based WFQ (more complex; maybe follow-on).
- We should explicitly measure “short queue wait decomposition”: is it enqueue wait vs prefill service vs decode service? Otherwise TTFT changes are hard to attribute.
- If we end up with a 3-class future (short/medium/long), make sure we don’t paint ourselves into a corner with enum assumptions.

Notes to self (Sofia)
- Keep the story simple for operators: ‘flag on = protects interactive tail latency under mixed load’. Everything else is implementation detail.
- Don’t let the project slip into kernel wars; scheduler is the main lever for now.
